title: Higher-codimension residue transitions
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and $T$ a Noetherian excellent scheme with $\ell$ invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring]. Use costalks $C_{\bar t}M=R\Gamma_{\bar t}M$, roots-of-unity twists, and normalized immediate residue transitions as specified in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. A geometric specialization $\bar u\rightsquigarrow\bar v$ is a map of strict localizations over $T$ [def-weil-geometric-point, def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]; its codimension $c$ is the dimension of the reduced closure of its general point in the strict localization at its special point. For every $M\in D^+(T_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$ and $a\in\mathbf Z$ there is a natural transition
$$\operatorname{sp}_{\bar u,\bar v}:H^a(C_{\bar u}M)\longrightarrow H^{a+2c}(C_{\bar v}M(c)).$$
For $c=1$ it is the normalized residue transition of the cited definition; for $c=0$ it is the transport for the specified geometric specialization. These maps are compatible with composition: for composable geometric specializations of codimensions $c,d$, the composite transition, with its intervening twist and degree shift, is the transition for their composite, of codimension $c+d$. In particular they give the same composite along two sides of any commutative square of geometric specializations. A specialization can be factored into a finite chain of immediate specializations (and a codimension-zero transport), and its transition is independent of the chosen factorization.

source.place: Expose XVII, Theorem 3.1.2 and section 3.5 (general transitions, naturality, transitivity and independence of factorization); geometric codimension and immediate specializations as in XIV section 2.1.
